cards.front: An {{c1::allele}} is one version of a gene, such as an allele for purple or white flowers in a pea plant.
cards.quote: An allele is one version of a gene, such as an allele for purple or white flowers in a pea plant.

cards.front: The two chromosomes of a pair are {{c1::homologous chromosomes}}: they carry the same genes in the same order but may carry different versions.
cards.quote: The two chromosomes of a pair are homologous chromosomes: they carry the same genes in the same order but may carry different versions.

cards.front: What is the difference between a diploid cell and a haploid cell?
cards.back: A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent. A haploid cell has one set.
cards.quote: A cell with two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent, is diploid.

cards.front: A {{c1::gamete}} is a sex cell, an egg or a sperm, and in humans it is haploid, with 23 chromosomes.
cards.quote: A gamete is a sex cell, an egg or a sperm, and in humans it is haploid, with 23 chromosomes.

cards.front: After DNA copying, each chromosome is two {{c1::sister chromatids}}: identical copies joined together.
cards.quote: Each chromosome is then two sister chromatids, identical copies joined together

cards.front: In meiosis, how many times is the DNA copied, and how many times does the cell divide?
cards.back: The DNA is copied once, and the cell divides twice. No DNA copying happens between the two divisions.
cards.why: Copying once and dividing twice is what cuts the chromosome number in half.
cards.quote: Key idea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, first separating the pairs and then the copies, so each sex cell gets one chromosome from each pair.

cards.front: A model cell starts with six chromosomes in three pairs. Just after DNA copying, how many chromosomes and how many chromatids does it hold?
cards.back: Six chromosomes and 12 chromatids. Joined sister chromatids count as one chromosome, so copying doubles the chromatids but not the chromosomes.
cards.quote: There are still six chromosomes because joined sister chromatids count as one chromosome.

cards.front: In meiosis, what separates in the first division, and what separates in the second?
cards.back: First division: the two homologous chromosomes of each pair separate. Second division: the sister chromatids separate.
cards.quote: Key idea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, first separating the pairs and then the copies, so each sex cell gets one chromosome from each pair.

cards.front: A model cell with 8 chromosomes (4 pairs) copies its DNA and finishes the first division of meiosis. How many cells are there, and how many chromosomes does each hold? What are the numbers after the second division?
cards.back: After the first division: 2 cells, each with 4 chromosomes (each still made of two joined chromatids). After the second: 4 cells, each with 4 chromosomes.
cards.why: The first division separates pairs, which halves the number. The second separates copies, so the count stays at 4.
cards.quote: Key idea: Meiosis copies the DNA once and divides twice, first separating the pairs and then the copies, so each sex cell gets one chromosome from each pair.

cards.front: Why does a human egg or sperm carry 23 chromosomes instead of 46?
cards.back: Fertilization joins two sets of 23 to make a diploid cell with 46 again.
cards.quote: Their two sets of 23 make a diploid cell with 46 again.

cards.front: A parent has two different alleles, A and a, of one gene. What is the chance that a given sex cell from this parent carries A?
cards.back: 50 percent. A sex cell gets only one chromosome from each pair, and it is equally likely to get either one.
cards.quote: So if a parent has two different alleles of a gene, each sex cell has a 50 percent chance of getting either one.

cards.front: In meiosis, which chromatids exchange matching pieces in crossing over, and in which division?
cards.back: Non-sister chromatids of paired homologous chromosomes exchange matching pieces during the first division (meiosis I).
cards.quote: In crossing over, non-sister chromatids of paired homologous chromosomes exchange matching pieces during meiosis I.

cards.front: What is independent assortment?
cards.back: Each pair of chromosomes lines up and separates on its own, whatever the other pairs do.
cards.quote: In independent assortment, each pair lines up and separates on its own, whatever the other pairs do.

cards.front: A pea plant has 7 chromosome pairs. Ignoring crossing over, how many different chromosome combinations can one of its sex cells carry?
cards.back: 2 to the power 7 = 128. Each of the 7 pairs doubles the count.
cards.quote: number of chromosome combinations in a sex cell = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of chromosome pairs

cards.front: An organism gains one extra chromosome pair, so n goes from 4 to 5. By what factor does the number of chromosome combinations in its sex cells change, ignoring crossing over?
cards.back: It doubles: from 2⁴ = 16 to 2⁵ = 32. Each extra pair doubles the count.
cards.quote: Thirty-two. Five doublings give 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁵ = 32.

cards.front: Two genes sit very close together on the same chromosome. Will they be shuffled independently of each other by independent assortment? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Genes close together on one chromosome tend to travel together. Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.
cards.quote: Genes close together on one chromosome tend to travel together, so independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.

cards.front: For one human parent, 2²³ is about 8.4 million combinations. Why do two sex cells from the same parent still almost never match, and why is 2ⁿ an undercount?
cards.back: 2ⁿ counts only the shuffling of whole chromosomes by independent assortment. Crossing over also swaps pieces between paired chromosomes, which adds far more mixes. So nearly every sex cell carries a new mix of alleles.
cards.why: This rests on the 2ⁿ rule plus the crossing over rule.
cards.quote: These are possibilities across many meioses, not children anyone could have, and they ignore crossing over, which adds far more.

cards.front: Why do brothers and sisters differ, while identical twins match so closely?
cards.back: Siblings grow from different eggs and different sperm, and each sex cell is a new mix of alleles. Identical twins come from one fertilized egg.
cards.quote: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg, which is why they match so closely.

cards.front: What does meiosis make from a diploid cell?
cards.back: Haploid cells. In animals these become gametes.
cards.quote: Meiosis makes haploid cells from a diploid cell.

cards.front: Compare mitosis and meiosis: purpose, and number and kind of cells made.
cards.back: Mitosis makes two matching cells for growth and repair. Meiosis usually makes four varied haploid cells (one egg in females) for making gametes.
cards.quote: Key idea: Mitosis makes two matching cells for growth and repair; meiosis makes four varied haploid cells, and that variety helps a population face a changing environment.
cards.section: Explain: mitosis and meiosis side by side

cards.front: What creates new alleles, and what does meiosis do with alleles?
cards.back: Mutations, rare copying mistakes, make new alleles. Crossing over and shuffling mix alleles into new combinations. Meiosis itself does not create new alleles.
cards.quote: Mutations make new alleles; crossing over and shuffling mix them into new combinations.
cards.section: Explain: mitosis and meiosis side by side

cards.front: How do offspring of asexual reproduction compare genetically with their parent?
cards.back: They are genetically the same as the parent. Sexual reproduction makes offspring that differ.
cards.quote: Asexual reproduction, with one parent and mitosis-like division, makes offspring that are genetically the same as the parent.
cards.section: Explain: mitosis and meiosis side by side

cards.front: When conditions change, does high genetic diversity guarantee that a population survives? What does it do?
cards.back: No. It raises the chance that some members survive and reproduce, but it does not guarantee survival.
cards.quote: when conditions change it raises the chance that some members survive and reproduce, but it does not guarantee survival.
cards.section: Explain: mitosis and meiosis side by side

cards.front: Would sexual reproduction help yeast populations kept in a comfortable environment that never changes?
cards.back: Not necessarily. In a 2012 experiment, sex gave no overall advantage at a comfortable 30 °C, but sexual populations adapted more at a stressful 37 °C with added salt.
cards.quote: In a 2012 experiment, sexual yeast populations adapted more than asexual ones at a stressful 37 °C with added salt, but at a comfortable 30 °C sex gave no overall advantage.
cards.section: Explain: mitosis and meiosis side by side

cards.front: A dog has 39 chromosome pairs and a human has 23. How many more pairs does the dog have, and about how many times more chromosome combinations per sex cell does that give?
cards.back: 16 more pairs. Each pair doubles the count, so 2¹⁶ = 65,536 times more combinations (about 5.5 × 10¹¹ versus 8.4 × 10⁶).
cards.quote: A dog has 39 pairs and a human has 23. How many more pairs does the dog have, and about how many times more combinations does that give?

cards.front: Human egg and embryo samples averaged 41.6 crossovers, while donor sperm averages ran from 22.2 to 28.1. Why can you not conclude from this that eggs have more crossovers than sperm?
cards.back: The studies used different people and methods, so they are not a controlled egg-versus-sperm comparison. The numbers are suggestive, not a test of the difference.
cards.quote: The studies used different people and methods, so they are not a controlled egg-versus-sperm comparison.

cards.front: In a yeast experiment comparing sexual and asexual populations in a hot, salty environment, why also grow both kinds in a comfortable environment?
cards.back: To tell whether the benefit of sex depends on the environment. A gain only in the harsh environment would support the idea that sex helps most when conditions are harsh.
cards.quote: Controls: run both kinds of population in a comfortable environment too, so you can tell whether the benefit depends on the environment.

cards.front: A yeast design keeps each environment (comfortable or hot and salty) the same for every generation. Can it test whether sex helps a population cope with a changing environment?
cards.back: No. Both environments stay the same throughout, so it tests harshness, not change. It could only support the idea that sex helps most when conditions are harsh.
cards.quote: Both environments stay the same throughout, so this design does not test a changing environment.
